contests.short_description: Public Safety Services Levy Lid Lift
ballot_title: The City Council of the City of Lake Forest Park adopted Resolution No. 26-2084 to fund Public Safety Services.

This proposition would fund Public Safety Services per the Resolution including police services, safety equipment, 911 dispatch, emergency management services, jail services, and mental health crisis response by temporarily setting the maximum total regular levy rate at $0.88920/$1,000 for collection in 2027, with annual increases for five years based on inflation (Seattle region CPI-U). Qualifying low-income seniors, disabled veterans, and other disabled persons are exempt under RCW 84.36.381.
Should this proposition be approved?
explanatory_statement: The City of Lake Forest Park proposes Proposition 1 to provide sustainable funding for Public Safety Services including: police staffing, training, and safety equipment; 911 dispatch services; jail services; prosecution and public defense costs; and crisis intervention and mental health response programs.

Proposition 1 would temporarily authorize an annual increase of approximately $1.2 million in the City’s regular property tax levy through a levy lid lift. Without a voter approved levy lid lift, the City is limited to increasing its tax levy by 1%. The additional levy funds from Proposition 1 would be tracked separately and could only be used to pay for the cost of Public Safety Services.

Proposition 1 would cost property owners $0.22 per $1,000 of assessed valuation ($22 per $100,000). In 2027, for a $963,000 median value home this would be about $211.86 annually or $17.66 per month. For each of the next five years (2028 – 2032), the levy lid lift could be increased by the rate of inflation, which requires an open public process and a council vote to approve.

Proposition 1 exempts qualifying seniors, disabled veterans and others with disabilities from the levy increase. When Proposition 1 expires, the levy will decrease to what it would have been if never approved and the City had only taken the 1% increase authorized by state law.
For questions about this measure, contact: Phillip Hill, City Administrator, (206) 368-5440, phill@cityoflfp.gov
argument_for: Lake Forest Park faces the same difficult choices that other communities across the state face, concocted by Tim Eyman and maintained by the State Legislature. While inflation has increased annually by 2.8% and by over 5% recently, revenues have been hamstrung by a 1% annual cap on property tax increases.
As the years have ticked by, cities have struggled to fund basic operations. Some have reduced staffing. Brier cut police department funding. Edmonds explored selling off parks.

Lake Forest Park staff project that our status quo will exhaust the general fund by 2031. While the city has cut costs by closing City Hall on Fridays, preserving current services requires further action. Our city government listened to feedback when designing this levy, ensuring transparency by moving the process through the Finance Committee. The City Council recognizing this crisis, unanimously voted to send this levy to us.

In voting down levies for decades, our beloved Lake Forest Park has been borrowing against the future. We are lucky to live here, and it is time for our votes to reflect the best of our values. To preserve our commitment to safety, community policing, and our environment, please vote Yes on Proposition 1.
argument_against: Fully funding public safety in Lake Forest Park is critical. As I told the police before last year’s vote, I’d happily vote for the tax increase if would increase the police budget. I support raising taxes to increase funds for public safety; unfortunately, the city has not committed to do that. Instead, they have only committed to spend the $1M per year tax increase on public safety, with no commitment to add this additional amount to the current spending for public safety from the general fund.

The City exaggerates the budget struggles. The unrestricted general fund revenue increased by about $4M total, $1M per year, from 2021 to 2025, vastly more than the $35k the city implies because property tax is not the only source of general funds. The City describes a ~$400k structural deficit, yet has added, rather than cut, non-safety personnel. New hires cost an amount similar to the current deficit.
A ‘no’ vote does not threaten our public safety. It directs the city to restrain non-safety spending and commit to increasing funds for our police and public safety personnel.
rebuttal_by_opponents: No statement submitted.
rebuttal_by_proponents: Inflation has hit the city's public safety budget hard. The costs of 911, jail, legal services, and policing have risen dramatically recently, and the city has drawn down one-time general funds to fill the gap. Maintaining our service levels requires additional revenue.
We vote our values when electing a council to protect what we care about. Let's give city government and staff the tools to deliver these priorities and hold them accountable to it.

contests.title: City of SeaTac - Proposition No. 1

source.name: WA Secretary of State voters' guide

contests.short_description: Fire Prevention and Criminal Justice Sales and Use Tax
ballot_title: The City Council of the City of SeaTac passed Ordinance No. 26-1017 concerning funding for public safety and other City services. If approved, this proposition would increase the City’s sales and use tax rate by 1/10th of 1% (0.1%) to provide funding for public safety services, including but not limited to, fire protection, fire prevention and emergency medical response; law enforcement support and staffing and retention; criminal justice purposes; public safety operations, maintenance and capital; and other public safety operations and services authorized under RCW 82.14.450. Should this proposition be approved?
explanatory_statement: The City of SeaTac provides public safety and related services directly and through contracts with the Puget Sound Regional Fire Authority and King County Sheriff’s Office. These services support residents and thousands of people who travel to SeaTac daily to access local hotels, restaurants, businesses, employment opportunities, and the Seattle-Tacoma International Airport, located entirely within the City.

This influx produces a daily visitor population more than six times the City’s residential population. Serving residents and travelers results in a disproportionately high number of complex fire and emergency medical incidents and increases demands on public safety services. Inflation and hazardous workplace conditions have increased the cost of these services. City revenues have not kept pace, and additional resources are needed to continue providing critical fire, medical and public safety services.

Proposition 1 would authorize a 0.1% sales and use tax on taxable retail sales and uses within SeaTac. The tax would apply to taxable purchases by residents and travelers. Only transactions taxable under Washington law would be taxed; most groceries are exempt. State law also exempts motor vehicle sales and the first 36 months of vehicle leases from this tax. Revenue from the tax would be shared 85% to the City and 15% to King County. At least one-third of the revenue would be used solely for fire protection purposes, criminal justice purposes, or both, as required by RCW 82.14.450. This tax would add $0.10 to a taxable $100 purchase.
For questions about this measure, contact: Cindy Corsilles, City Attorney, (206) 973-4662, cityclerk@seatacwa.gov
argument_for: The City of SeaTac is a unique community. Every day, thousands of workers, travelers, visitors, and airport users come into our city, creating demands on public safety services including police, fire, and emergency medical response. These services protect everyone who lives, works, visits, and does business in SeaTac.

Proposition 1 provides a fair way to fund essential services. Rather than placing the burden solely on SeaTac residents, this modest 0.1% Public Safety sales tax asks everyone who makes taxable purchases in our community to contribute—including visitors, travelers, workers who use and benefit from services.

Our city provides public safety services to a community that is far larger each day than the number of people who live here. It is only fair that the people who come to SeaTac and rely on our public safety system also contribute to keeping those services strong.

By acting now, the City of SeaTac has the opportunity to keep and maintain local control over how locally generated revenue is used. If King County were to impose its own public safety sales tax first, SeaTac would receive a smaller share of that revenue and have less control over its use. Vote Yes on Proposition 1
argument_against: The people of SeaTac are awake and watching—again. In 2014, the City Council and staff imposed a utility tax on electricity, cable, internet, phone, and more. In 2015, voters replaced that council, the utility tax was repealed, and the City Manager fired. The new council even rejected the automatic property-tax increase. That began ten years of fiscal accountability, new sidewalks, surplus funds, and increased police staffing to keep SeaTac safe.

Since then, most of the City Council has been replaced by people with a different agenda. The surplus is gone, spending out of control, and now they want to raise taxes again—this time on our local businesses. A thriving business community has helped make SeaTac one of the most affordable cities in King County. Don’t kill the goose that lays the golden eggs and price ourselves out of our own community. What’s next—another utility tax or property-tax increase? The council and staff are flirting with their own jobs—again
Please don’t be fooled. The B&O tax is a red flag for what could be coming if we don’t change course. We’ve done it before, we can do it again.
Vote No on this tax increase!
rebuttal_by_opponents: A Public Safety Sales Tax is even higher than a B&O tax. Those, and new utility taxes, were all planned for at the same council meeting. This council and staff have a spending problem—SeaTac residents are already taxed to death. The Airport is a red herring. The largest transactions at the airport—airline tickets—are exempt from sales tax. These new taxes are regressive and hurt residents.
For all our sakes, Vote No!
rebuttal_by_proponents: Proposition 1 this is not a tax on SeaTac residents or local businesses. It is the best tool we have to recover revenue from the thousands of travelers who visit SeaTac every year. In a time of unprecedented increase in public safety costs, it is the best way to ensure that residents and visitors alike continue to have reliable public safety and emergency services.

contests.title: City of Seattle - Proposition No. 1

source.name: WA Secretary of State voters' guide

ballot_title: The City of Seattle adopted Ordinance No. 127474 concerning funding for transit service and related transportation needs in Seattle.

The City of Seattle’s Proposition 1 would dedicate funding to transit services benefiting Seattle residents, including more frequent service; affordable fare programs for qualifying individuals; reliability, access, and climate projects; enhanced service on RapidRide and routes serving regional centers and high equity priority areas; facilitation of Sound Transit expansion; and others as provided in Ordinance 127474. It authorizes a 0.3% sales and use tax for up to ten years to replace the current voter-approved 0.15% sales tax expiring March 31, 2027.
Should this Proposition be approved?
explanatory_statement: In 2020, Ordinance 126250 enacted a 0.15 percent, six-year sales and use tax for transportation purposes. The tax was enacted under authority granted to the City by Seattle voters in approving Ordinance 126115. The tax expires March 31, 2027.

To replace this funding, Proposition 1 proposes granting the City authority to enact a sales and use tax for transit purposes by a future ordinance, with a maximum rate of 0.3 percent and a maximum length of ten years. The new tax cannot take effect earlier than April 1, 2027.

Tax revenue would be only for purposes described in Ordinance 127474, including (among others): King County Metro services with over 65 percent of stops within Seattle; implementing King County Regional Transit Safety Task Force recommendations; service hours on current and future RapidRide lines serving Seattle, connections to regional centers, and routes serving high equity priority areas; programs supporting transit access for qualifying seniors, individuals with disabilities, residents of low-income housing, youth and young adults, students, and others; planning for and deployment of increased electric transit in certain pollution-impacted communities; transit infrastructure maintenance and capital improvements; and staffing of programs to facilitate Sound Transit 3 projects.

The Seattle Transit Advisory Board will serve as the public oversight committee charged with advising on spending of Proposition 1 revenues. Annual and midterm City reports, as well as reports requested in partnership with King County Metro, will evaluate the effectiveness of money spent and services provided.
For questions about this measure, contact: Polly Grow, Seattle Ethics and Elections Commission, (206) 615-1248, polly.grow@seattle.gov
argument_for: Seattle needs great transit. Without it, riders with disabilities, older adults, youth, and working families are stuck waiting for the bus and miss opportunities. Transit should be a seamless part of peoples’ lives, not a burden to plan around.

In 2020, we voted to improve bus service across Seattle. That measure has delivered: buses run more often, and 10,000 of our neighbors receive free transit passes. But this funding runs out in 2027 unless we renew it.

For just $29 more per year per household, Proposition 1 will ensure buses come more often, later at night, and on weekends. It will double the free passes for low income Seattleites. With buses we can count on, more families can skip the expense of gas or a second car. And we can all enjoy less traffic and cleaner air. Vote “Yes” to keep Seattle's buses coming.

Endorsed by Mayor Katie Wilson, King County Executive Girmay Zahilay, Seattle City Councilmembers Hollingsworth, Saka, Foster, Juarez, Kettle, Lin, Rinck, Rivera, and Saka, King County Councilmembers Barón, Dembowski, Lewis and Mosqueda, MLK Labor, ATU 587, King County Democrats, Seattle Streets Alliance, 350 Seattle, Transit Riders Union, Transportation Choices Coalition, The Urbanist, and more.
argument_against: Seattle politicians say they care about affordability, then ask residents to approve another regressive sales tax. Proposition 1 would double the Seattle Transit Measure sales tax from 0.15% to 0.30%, putting our sales tax at 10.7%, among the highest rates of any major city in America. Before demanding more from taxpayers, government should demonstrate accountability for the money it already receives.

The measure includes funding connected to Sound Transit, even as the agency struggles to deliver projects voters were promised. Ballard and West Seattle residents have paid Sound Transit taxes for years while planned light-rail expansions face enormous financial challenges and uncertainty. Meanwhile, transit agencies are leaving fare revenue uncollected. At least one-third of riders on Sound Transit boarded without paying during the World Cup. Taxpayers should not continually be asked to pay more while agencies fail to collect fares from riders.

Seattle families already face high housing, food, utility, and transportation costs. Sales taxes disproportionately burden working families and people with lower incomes because they consume a larger share of household earnings. Reliable transit matters. So does accountability. City Hall should prioritize existing resources, demand responsible management, and improve fare collection before raising taxes.
Vote No on Proposition 1.
rebuttal_by_opponents: The proponents call Proposition 1 “just $29 more,” but that minimizes the real issue: Seattle’s sales tax would climb to 10.7%, hitting working families and low-income residents hardest. Doubling this regressive tax is not affordability.

Reliable transit deserves responsible management. Before demanding more, City Hall and transit agencies should prioritize existing revenue, collect unpaid fares, and prove taxpayers are getting results. Seattleites already pay heavily for promised transit projects. Vote no until accountability comes first.
rebuttal_by_proponents: This measure funds bus service from King County Metro. Voting no cuts bus service working people rely on. Without it, late night and shift workers lose out. This measure helps us afford to live in our expensive city.
The measure costs a low income household $17 a year. Owning a car costs $11,577 a year. Proposition 1 provides free ORCA cards to 22,000 of the lowest income riders. Vote yes on Proposition 1.
contests.committee_for: Kirk Hovenkotter, Kathryn Ricchiuto, Nick Sattele, info@hoponboardseattle.org

contests.title: City of Shoreline - Proposition No. 1

source.name: WA Secretary of State voters' guide

contests.short_description: Formation of the Shoreline Metropolitan Park District
ballot_title: The Shoreline City Council adopted Resolution No. 562 concerning the creation of a metropolitan park district in Shoreline.

This proposition would create the Shoreline Metropolitan Park District to finance and refinance the acquisition, construction, operation, maintenance, programming, renovation, and expansion of a pool facility and future recreational facilities. The District, with the same boundaries as Shoreline, governed by a Board composed of City Councilmembers, would exercise powers in state law, provide ongoing funding, levy regular property taxes not to exceed $0.75/$1,000 assessed valuation (anticipated initial rate $0.55/$1,000, or as necessary to generate approximately $8.8 million annually).
Should the Shoreline Metropolitan Park District be formed?
explanatory_statement: If approved by voters, this proposition creates the Shoreline Metropolitan Park District (MPD) to finance and refinance the construction, operation, and maintenance of a new indoor pool facility and potential future recreational facilities. The MPD would have the same boundaries as the City of Shoreline (City). The MPD would be a new taxing jurisdiction (RCW 35.61) governed by a board composed of City Councilmembers. City staff would operate and maintain the pool pursuant to an agreement with the MPD.

The approximately 48,000 square foot facility would be built on City-owned property at 17828 Midvale Ave N. The preliminary accessible design includes an 8-lane lap pool with diving well; recreation pool with a lazy river for walking and floating; warmer hydrotherapy pool; sauna; universal changerooms; party rooms; parking; and outdoor spaces connecting to the Interurban Trail.

Creating the MPD would allow for construction of future recreational facilities should additional funding be available. The pool facility design leaves space for a potential recreation facility addition.

The anticipated initial property tax levy rate is $0.55/$1,000 assessed valuation, or as necessary to generate approximately $8.8 million annually. The maximum allowable rate is $0.75/$1,000. Revenue would pay for pool facility construction, operation, and maintenance. Revenue could only be used for the pool facility and future recreational facilities, not other City needs.
Tax collection would start in 2028. A homeowner with a median value home ($831,000 in 2026) would pay approximately $421 per year, an average of $35 per month, in additional property taxes.
For questions about this measure, contact: Eric Bratton, Communications Program Manager, (206) 801-2217, ebratton@shorelinewa.gov
argument_for: It’s Time Shoreline! Let’s invest in our future. Imagine kids learning water safety, teenagers competing in swim meets, adults enjoying lap swims, and seniors staying healthy through supportive water exercise. Take a float through the lazy river while neighbors take fitness classes and build community. A well-planned aquatics facility through Proposition 1 will provide a safe, accessible home base for high school swim teams and a welcoming gathering place for residents of all ages.

Studies show that formal swimming lessons reduce drowning risk in young children by 88% while aquatic exercise improves strength, mobility, and fall prevention in older adults. A local pool prepares our youth to safely explore Washington's waters and helps keep aging residents active.

Shoreline residents shouldn’t have to leave town or pay higher non-resident fees for pool access. Creating a Metropolitan Park District (MPD) establishes stable, dedicated local funding to build, operate, and maintain an affordable, year-round facility right here at home.

Equitably funded through property taxes, this measure invests directly in health, safety, and community well-being. Make a difference today. Vote yes on Proposition 1 for a healthy vision of Shoreline’s future. The future is now!
argument_against: A Permanent Tax Hike for a $100 Million Luxury Pool? Shoreline voters need to consider this proposal carefully. We cannot afford to get this wrong.

This measure creates a new Metropolitan Park District with the power to permanently raise local/city property taxes by at least 33% — all to fund a $100 million pool facility to start. But this is not a temporary bond. It's a permanent tax, and it hands the newly created Metropolitan Park District sweeping authority to fund future projects without ever coming back to voters for approval.
Every resident pays the price. Property owners foot the bill directly, and landlords will no doubt pass the cost straight through to renters in the form of higher rent.

Shoreline wants you to pay $100 million for just a luxury pool facility – no recreation center, no fitness center, no senior center, no commercial kitchen. It’s way too much money for too little that will benefit too few. The city has more pressing priorities that should be addressed with any future tax increase. Don’t create a new tax district that gives the city a blank check. Proposition 1 will make Shoreline less affordable for all forever. Vote no.
rebuttal_by_opponents: This is no time to add $100M in debt for a pool facility and saddle taxpayers with a 33% local tax increase. These are extremely uncertain economic times with high interest rates and rising inflation.

Numerous other tax increases are already approved or expected in the next 2-3 years. Recent property tax increases have far outpaced inflation. There’s a limit to what taxpayers can afford. Prioritization of limited tax dollars is crucial. Vote no.
rebuttal_by_proponents: The Con statement is fundamentally inaccurate. The MPD wouldn’t have sweeping tax authority; it is limited between 55 and 75 cents per $1,000 assessed. Their claim that the MPD will increase property taxes by 33% is false. It would increase approximately 5.5% to 7.5%.
Rather than a luxury expense, the measure simply replaces the pool we enjoyed from 1971 to 2020. Fearmongering + incorrect arithmetic = a bad argument. Vote yes.
contests.committee_for: Krishnakant Nammi, Susie McDowell, Buddy Smith, letshorelineswim.org
contests.committee_against: Sandra Cribbs, Jeff Hays, Joseph Smith, www.shorelineprop1.com
options: For the formation of a Shoreline Metropolitan Park District to be governed by Shoreline City Councilmembers.
Against the formation of a Shoreline Metropolitan Park District.

contests.title: Auburn School District No. 408 - Proposition No. 1

source.name: WA Secretary of State voters' guide

ballot_title: The Board of Directors of Auburn School District No. 408 has approved Resolution No. 1426, concerning a proposition to finance construction of new and replacement schools. This proposition would authorize the District to provide funds to construct a new Middle School and replace Cascade Middle School and Alpac Elementary, to increase capacity and reduce class sizes, modernize technology and learning environments, improve safety and security, and renovate playfields for student and community use, by issuing up to $491,000,000 of general obligation bonds maturing within 20 years, and levying annual excess property taxes to repay the bonds, as the resolution provides.
Should this proposition be:
explanatory_statement: Passage of Proposition 1 enables Auburn School District to finance the construction of new and replacement schools by issuing up to $491,000,000 of general obligation bonds. If voters approve this proposition, the District will use the bond proceeds to (1) construct and equip a new Middle School #5, (2) construct and equip a new middle school with enlarged capacity to replace Cascade Middle School, and (3) construct and equip a new elementary school with enlarged capacity to replace Alpac Elementary School. These projects will increase school capacity, reduce class sizes and the use of portable classrooms, improve safety and security, modernize technology and student learning environments, improve energy efficiency, and improve and expand playfields and athletic facilities for student and community use.

If voters approve this proposition, the District expects to receive approximately $36,248,500 in construction assistance funds from the State to complete these projects. The bonds will mature within 20 years and be repaid from annual excess property tax levies. The District’s website at www.auburn.wednet.edu/2026election has the anticipated tax impact associated with this bond. A property tax exemption may be available to senior or disabled homeowners who meet specified income limits. For information regarding exemptions, call the King County Assessor at (206) 296-3920.
For questions about this measure, contact: Cindi Blansfield, Associate Superintendent, (253) 931-4930, cblansfield@auburn.wednet.edu
argument_for: Vote Yes to build a brand-new middle school and replace the aging, outdated Cascade Middle School and Alpac Elementary. Today, over 1,100 of our middle schoolers are crowded into 45 temporary portables, while Alpac faces constant, costly repairs. This bond directly solves overcrowding district-wide in the middle schools.

Our community and students deserve modern facilities now—not years down the road. Clean, safe, and modern schools ignite student pride, boost teacher commitment, and uplift entire neighborhoods. Our kids deserve spaces designed for success.

This is a fiscally responsible investment. Auburn School District has a proven track record of delivering projects on time and under budget while keeping taxes low. At an estimated cost of just $1.10 per $1,000 of assessed value—about $50.41 a month for a $550,000 home—we can secure three modern schools to serve generations.
A majority voted Yes in the last election, but we need a 60% supermajority to secure critical state matching funds. Our students cannot wait.
argument_against: The Auburn School District is demanding a massive $491 million bond package to build three local schools, averaging a staggering $163 million per individual facility. Meanwhile, the neighboring Tacoma School District is successfully building eight separate schools for an average total cost of $66 million each.

The new Lowell and Whittier are modern, state-of-the-art elementary schools for under $50 million each. However, Auburn demands a whopping $118 million to demolish, design & build Alpac Elementary. This massive cost discrepancy begs an obvious question: where exactly is the other $68 million going for this school alone?

Furthermore, the district's advertised $1.10 property tax rate completely fails to cover repaying the $491 million principal plus the $350+ million in interest debt. Repaying this massive accumulated interest forces true initial rates up to $1.93 per $1,000, exposing a huge gap between the advertised numbers and the harsh financial reality.

Working families and honest local people are barely getting by in today's tough economic environment. The school district must bring local taxpayers a reasonable, fiscally responsible request instead of pushing over-inflated, expensive dreams that place an unfair, heavy financial burden on our entire community. Vote No
rebuttal_by_opponents: If you own property assessed at $600,000, your current property tax bill for schools alone is $4,800. If you add this bond at the true cost of $1.93 per $1,000, your school tax portion will jump to $5,958 per year.

Tacoma's approved $650 million bond replaces or renovates 11 aging schools; Auburn wants $491 million for just 3. Don't be bullied, make them resubmit this with real cost, not bloated numbers. Vote no.
rebuttal_by_proponents: Misleading comparisons ignore differences in school size, site conditions, and long-term construction standards. Auburn is building schools designed to last a century and has a proven record of completing projects on time and on budget. Replacing aging schools and overcrowded portables now is a smarter long-term investment than continuing costly repairs. Vote Yes to provide safe, modern schools for generations of Auburn students.

contests.title: Highline School District No. 401 - Proposition No. 1

source.name: WA Secretary of State voters' guide

contests.short_description: Bonds to Replace and Rebuild Deteriorating Schools and Improve Safety
ballot_title: The Board of Directors of Highline School District No. 401 adopted Resolution No. 11-26, concerning neighborhood school improvements and safety upgrades. This proposition would authorize the District to: replace or rebuild four deteriorating schools (Cascade, Chinook, Sylvester, CHOICE Academy), including new career/technical learning spaces, secure entrances, security camera upgrades; make critical districtwide core building system upgrades, including heating, roofing, electrical, plumbing; implement districtwide health, security, fire system and earthquake safety upgrades; issue $595,400,000 of general obligation bonds maturing within 21 years; and levy annual excess property taxes to repay the bonds, all as provided in Resolution No. 11-26. Should this proposition be:
explanatory_statement: Proposition 1 authorizes school construction bonds to replace and rebuild deteriorating schools and make districtwide safety and accessibility improvements and upgrades. Proposition 1 will improve student, staff and community safety, security and accessibility, enhance student learning environments, improve and expand educational opportunities, and provide necessary student educational facilities (including career/technical learning spaces).

The bonds will allow Highline Public Schools to: (1) address critical needs districtwide, including core building system upgrades and site improvements (plumbing, hot water systems, HVAC, electrical, roofing, security, fire systems and earthquake safety upgrades); (2) construct a new school to replace Sylvester Middle School; (3) construct a new school to replace Cascade Middle School; (4) partially rebuild and modernize Chinook Middle School (replacing the oldest, most outdated buildings, facilities and infrastructure with new construction; renovating and updating existing usable buildings; and replacing portables with permanent classrooms); (5) rebuild and modernize the former Southern Heights Elementary School site as a new facility for CHOICE Academy; and (6) develop design plans for construction, redevelopment or replacement of Valley View Early Learning Center and Hilltop Elementary School. More information is available at highlineschools.org/bondandlevy.

The $595,400,000 of general obligation bonds will be repaid from annual excess property taxes sufficient to pay bond debt service over a maximum term of 21 years. Exemptions from taxes may be available to certain homeowners. For more information, contact the King County Department of Assessments, 206-296-3920.
For questions about this measure, contact: Andrew Burgess, Controller, (206) 631-3201, andrew.burgess@highlineschools.org
argument_for: Highline students deserve schools that are safe, healthy, and equipped for today’s learning. Vote yes on Prop. 1 to rebuild aging schools, address critical repairs, and make schools ADA accessible and more secure from safety threats.

This bond will provide all middle school students in our community with secure, modern classrooms. It would replace Cascade and Sylvester middle schools, rebuild Chinook Middle School, and rebuild Southern Heights for CHOICE Academy. It ensures an equal middle school educational environment for students in every Highline neighborhood.

Voting Yes protects our community’s investments in public facilities. As roofs, heating, plumbing, and electrical systems age, repairs become more costly, and facilities failures disrupt student learning. The bond is a practical investment that ensures safe, reliable facilities for students and our community for decades to come.

Local bonds are the only way to fund school construction and repairs. The state doesn’t provide this funding. Highline has a decades-long track record of completing projects on time and on budget. Quality schools strengthen neighborhoods and make communities safer. Please join parents, educators, neighbors and community leaders in voting yes on Prop. 1 so all Highline students can learn in safe, modern schools.
argument_against: Vote No for Now on Highline’s record-breaking $595.4 million bond proposal. If passed, taxpayers will have approved more than $1.4 billion in construction debt in just ten years. Meanwhile, Highline spends more than $25,000 per student annually, $3,000 more than the state average. Yet 67% of students test below grade level in reading, and 76% fail math and science grade level standards.
Even at newly rebuilt schools, state data shows worsening attendance and declining academic performance. New buildings may look impressive, but bricks and mortar cannot fix failing academics.

The district wants to rebuild three middle schools at once. Why not begin with two and return later for the third? A smaller bond would improve schools while keeping costs more manageable. With the cost of living climbing rapidly, families cannot afford this unnecessary burden.

Students deserve safe schools and strong academics. Taxpayers deserve responsible spending, transparency, and accountability. Highline has ignored community concerns and failed to earn our trust. Why should we trust the district with a bond this large? Send Highline back to the drawing board. Demand a smaller, smarter bond that puts students first and gives taxpayers a fair deal. Vote No for Now.
rebuttal_by_opponents: Safe & equitable schools shouldn’t require a $595.4M price tag. Real equity means safe facilities & academic progress, but even at new facilities, academics are falling. Massive construction debt isn't a practical or acceptable substitute for classroom learning.

Asking taxpayers for $161.3M for Chinook’s partial remodel - delayed until 2031- is not reasonable when full rebuilds at Sylvester ($180.3M) & Cascade ($172.1M) cost roughly the same. Demand smarter, more responsible planning: Vote No for Now!
rebuttal_by_proponents: Students attending Highline’s newly built schools have higher attendance and engagement. All students deserve safe, modern schools. We can’t afford to put off replacing aging, outdated schools while construction costs escalate, costing taxpayers much more later. Prop. 1 was shaped by a community-led advisory committee, recommending a practical plan focused on critical needs and responsible stewardship of tax dollars. Highline has earned our trust by delivering new schools on time, on budget. Please vote Yes!
contests.committee_for: Tina Orwall, Dan Satterberg, Sili Savusa, www.yesforHighline.org
contests.committee_against: Mike Bishoff, Kirsten Cooper, Katie Paulson, BetterPlanforHighline.com

ballot_title: The Board of Directors of Highline School District No. 401 adopted Resolution No. 12-26, concerning educational technology and capital improvements to maintain student learning. This proposition would fund districtwide technology, programs and staff and other capital improvements not funded by the State, including cybersecurity protections, reliable internet, technology operations and infrastructure, and student/staff technology access, and authorize the District to levy the following excess taxes on all taxable property within the District:
Collection Year
Estimated Levy Rate/$1,000 Assessed Value

all as provided in Resolution No. 12-26. Should this proposition be approved?
explanatory_statement: Proposition 2 authorizes a capital levy for educational technology and capital improvements to maintain student learning and improve student and staff safety and security. Proposition 2 will address the existing condition of educational technology equipment, infrastructure and systems and aging and educationally outdated school facilities.

The capital levy will fund: (1) cybersecurity protections and systems that protect student and staff data; (2) reliable internet, wireless networks and technology infrastructure that support teaching and learning; (3) student and staff devices, classroom technology and instructional software; (4) educator and staff training and support to implement technology improvements; and (5) other technology improvements and upgrades districtwide. The capital levy will also fund districtwide capital improvements to support the construction, modernization and remodeling of schools and facilities. More information is available at highlineschools.org/bondandlevy.

The proposed four-year levy would authorize collection of $12,000,000 in each of the years 2027 through 2030. The levy rate per $1,000 of assessed value required to produce these amounts is estimated to be $0.36 in 2027, $0.35 in 2028, $0.34 in 2029, and $0.32 in 2030. Exact levy rates will be determined based on actual assessed value at the time of levy.
Exemptions from taxes may be available to certain homeowners. For more information, contact the King County Department of Assessments, 206-296-3920.
For questions about this measure, contact: Andrew Burgess, Controller, (206) 631-3201, andrew.burgess@highlineschools.org
argument_for: Highline students and teachers rely on technology. Voting yes on Prop. 2 restores expired funding approved by voters for the secure systems, reliable internet, and classroom tools that prepare students for success.

This levy funds cybersecurity to protect sensitive student information. It pays for instructional software, internet access, teacher training for responsible technology use, technical support, and devices for students and staff. It funds the system that enables schools to reach parents in an emergency and for day-to-day communication. Technology costs are rising. The levy fills the gap between the funding provided by the state and the actual costs of meeting the technology needs of students and schools.

Modern, reliable technology is an essential investment in student learning. Students must learn safe, responsible use of the technology they encounter now and in the future. Reliable technology means students spend more time learning, and teachers spend more time teaching and less time waiting for systems to work.

The technology levy is a practical investment in the tools Highline students need today and the skills they will need to be successful in the future. Please join parents, educators, neighbors and community leaders in voting Yes for Highline by November 3.
argument_against: As Highline parents, we deeply support our public schools and want high-quality learning environments for every student. We also know that real student success comes from dedicated teachers, not screen time. We are voting No on this levy because our children and teachers deserve proven, human-led instruction over endless tech contracts.

Highline’s 1:1 device policy gives every child an internet-connected device starting in Kindergarten. While major urban districts and private schools are scaling back devices and auditing tech contracts, Highline is asking us to auto-renew. We need to pause and reassess how tech is being used in our classrooms.

Voters have approved multiple tech levies since 2018, yet academic outcomes have gone down. Relying on expensive and unproven programs like i-Ready instead of comprehensive, evidence-based instruction simply isn’t working. Furthermore, this levy is a blank check; with Policy 6101 just changed in June, it will give administrators upfront authority to sign million-dollar tech contracts without a public meeting or school board vote.

A No vote isn't abandoning our schools; it’s demanding smarter, low-tech learning and real district accountability before writing a $48 million check. Our students and our teachers deserve better. Vote No for Now.

Safe, working schools need transparent plans, not blank checks. Highline students deserve better.
rebuttal_by_proponents: This levy funds technology for student safety, parent communication, and cybersecurity - not more screentime. Fact check: Policy 6101 still requires school board approval of million-dollar tech contracts. Voters overwhelmingly approved Highline’s one/only tech levy in 2020. Vote yes: restore expired funding and give our students the same advantages as other communities.

explanatory_statement: Passage of Proposition 1 would allow Kent School District to replace an expiring voter-approved levy for school programs and operations by levying $104,700,000 for collection in 2028, $111,100,000 for collection in 2029, $115,700,000 for collection in 2030, and $121,400,000 for collection in 2031. The proposed levy would replace an existing levy that voters previously approved and expires in 2027. The expiring levy currently funds approximately 15% of the District’s general operating expenses. If approved, the proposed replacement levy would pay for day-to-day school operations to meet student needs not funded by the State, including but not limited to college and career readiness staff and programs, physical, social, and emotional learning staff and programs (including mental health counselors and staff), materials, supplies, and operational costs (including utilities and insurance), transportation, safety and security staff, athletic and extra-curricular programs, electives, and classroom support programs.

Based on projected assessed valuation information, the District estimates a tax rate of $1.95 per $1,000 of assessed valuation for 2028; $1.93 per $1,000 of assessed valuation for 2029; $1.88 per $1,000 of assessed valuation for 2030; and $1.84 per $1,000 of assessed valuation for 2031. A property tax exemption may be available to senior or disabled homeowners who meet specified income limits. For information regarding exemptions, call the King County Assessor at (206) 296-3920.
For questions about this measure, contact: Dr. Wade Barringer, Deputy Superintendent, (253) 373-7001, Wade.Barringer@kent.k12.wa.us
argument_for: Our schools are one of the most important investments our community makes—and this renewal levy will help keep that investment strong. It provides critical local funding that keeps schools safe, supports student learning, provides extracurricular opportunities, and helps ensure every child has access to the resources they need to succeed.

Voting Yes means continuing local funding that directly supports students, teachers, and programs not fully paid for by the state. This includes academic support, athletics, arts, mental health resources, music, safety, and transportation. This investment touches thousands of students and helps recruit and retain the outstanding teachers and staff who prepare these students for college, careers, and life.

Let’s renew our commitment to strong schools by voting Yes! Strong schools support local businesses, strengthen property values, and prepare the next generation of workers and leaders. This proposal continues a long tradition of local investment in our schools while maintaining one of the lowest school levy rates among neighboring districts.

This levy is not a new tax. It is a continued investment in educational opportunities today and in the strength of our community tomorrow. Please join us in voting Yes for our students, our schools, and our shared future.
argument_against: We all want strong schools and well-supported students, but writing a bigger check will not fix poor financial management. The district is asking for significantly more money while class sizes grow, enrollment declines, and families are left wondering where the money is actually going. We cannot continue to fund failing leadership while our students bear the burden of larger classes and reduced support.

District leadership has consistently turned a deaf ear to the community, and this levy comes with no binding promises to safeguard a single program or staffing group. Make no mistake: this tax hike will not bring back the vital resources cut this year, and it will not stop them from cutting more next year. We cannot keep writing blank checks to an administration that refuses to listen, consistently provides less than surrounding districts, and prioritizes themselves over students.

Furthermore, this levy is running a year ahead of schedule, with no effect on funding until 2028. Voting “No” now costs our classrooms nothing in 2027. Stand up for true accountability, new leadership, and better outcomes for our children. Vote no today, and let the district earn your trust with a community-aligned plan before trying again next year.
rebuttal_by_opponents: Supporters claim this levy will fund things like student supports, athletics, and the arts. The last levy promised those same things through 2027, but the district cut them this year.

Don’t accept empty promises. While taxes are rising, test scores and graduation rates are dropping, staffing is being cut, and class sizes are growing. Vote “No” today. Make the district earn your trust with a community-aligned plan and new leadership before trying again next year.
rebuttal_by_proponents: The opposition’s claims don’t match the facts. Kent School District has passed seven consecutive independent financial accountability audits and maintained a high credit rating—measurable signs of responsible financial management, not financial disarray.

This renewal levy isn’t a blank check. It provides funding for local schools, with accountability for every dollar. Our students deserve decisions based on facts and transparency, not misleading claims that undermine confidence in our schools and the people who serve them.

ballot_title: The Board of Fire Commissioners of King County Fire Protection District No. 20 adopted Resolution No. 2026-002, concerning emergency response facilities to protect public health, life and property. This proposition would authorize the District to: improve emergency response support facilities and infrastructure on two sites owned by the District; renovate and modernize the existing fire station; acquire firefighting and emergency response apparatus; issue no more than $16,000,000 of general obligation bonds maturing within 20 years; and levy annual excess property taxes to repay the bonds, all as provided in Resolution No. 2026-002. Should this proposition be:
explanatory_statement: King County Fire Protection District No. 20 provides fire suppression and rescue services, emergency medical services, and fire prevention and community education to protect life and property from the adverse effects of fires, medical emergencies or exposure to dangerous conditions.

The Board of Fire Commissioners has determined the inadequate size and aging and outdated facilities of the District, and the need to improve site security and resilience, operational readiness and efficiency, and community, firefighter and emergency responder safety, require the District to improve emergency response support facilities and infrastructure on two sites owned by the District. The improvements include renovating and modernizing the existing fire station, and acquiring firefighting and emergency response apparatus.

If approved, this proposition would authorize no more than $16,000,000 of general obligation bonds that would mature within a maximum of 20 years and be repaid from annual excess property taxes. The estimated tax rate is approximately $0.28 per $1,000 of assessed value. Exemptions from taxes may be available to certain homeowners. argument_for: As a neighborhood committee we support this bond because it is an investment in the safety and preparedness of our community. We deserve reliable emergency services, safe facilities for our firefighters, and the resources needed to meet future challenges.

Our firefighters respond to thousands of emergency calls from a station that was built more than 40 years ago and is not seismic approved. While the dedication of our firefighters has never changed, some of the facilities and apparatus they rely on every day have reached the end of their useful life and need replacing.

This bond will modernize Fire Station 20, replace an aging reserve engine, and improve the district's emergency operations campus by constructing nearby secure storage for emergency equipment and reserve apparatus. These projects/buildings will help protect emergency vehicles, supplies, improve firefighter safety, and ensure the district is prepared to respond to all emergencies and disasters.

The proposed bond is focused on long-term capital improvements that cannot be funded through the district's regular operating budget. By making these investments now, we can preserve and improve the facilities and equipment that support emergency response for years to come. Vote Yes on the KCFD No. 20 Community Safety Bond.

Judge Hawk is a trusted, experienced legal leader. Senators Murray and Cantwell appointed her to their federal judge selection committee. The American Bar Association selected her to observe Guantanamo Bay military hearings, and later chose her to assist families at the border torn apart by Trump-era immigration policies.

Judge Hawk has presided over hundreds of criminal, civil, and family law cases, as well as appeals from lower courts. She has never had a trial overturned for legal error. She follows the law. More than 100 current and retired judges and justices from across Washington endorse Judge Hawk.

Judge Hawk will bring a strong, independent voice. Endorsed by the National Women’s Political Caucus, local and county Democratic organizations, and the State Labor Council, she understands the concerns of women and working families and will bring that perspective to the Court. Judge Hawk will protect our rights and the rule of law.

statement.label: Legal/judicial experience
paragraphs: Judge, State Court of Appeals, appointed by Governor Jay Inslee, then elected. I am proud to serve the state’s second highest court, hearing cases statewide.

statement.label: Other professional experience

statement.label: Education
paragraphs: BA and JD, University of Washington

statement.label: Community service
paragraphs: More than 10 years service to King County Bar Association Neighborhood Legal Clinics, providing free legal assistance to people who could not afford an attorney. Many cases involved renters, consumers, and working families facing immediate financial or housing insecurity.

statement.label: Statement
paragraphs: I’m proud to be the only candidate in this position with statewide judicial experience and an appellate track record demonstrating respect for the rule of law, its impacts on communities, and all people we serve. With my background representing everyday Washingtonians, I will bring a unique perspective to the Supreme Court, where I’ll continue authoring opinions that are independent, fair, and grounded in shared values.

In every case I have taken as a lawyer, and heard as a judge, I have focused on the right of every person to equal access to justice, equal treatment under the law, and fair outcomes. I’ve written hundreds of decisions across civil, criminal, family, administrative, and constitutional law, an unmatched breadth of experience rated “exceptionally well qualified” by Washington Women Lawyers and the Cardozo Society.

I’m proudly endorsed by AG Nick Brown, Justices Gonzalez, Gordon-McCloud, Whitener, Montoya-Lewis, Mungia, Angelis, former Justices Ireland and Yu, over 100 judicial colleagues elected from all 39 counties in Washington, US Rep Pramila Jayapal, King County Exec Girmay Zahilay, WA State Labor Council, Machinists, Teachers, King County Democrats, and more.
Together, we can maintain the integrity and independence of our courts in challenging times. I ask for your vote.

statement.label: Legal/judicial experience
paragraphs: Judge on King County Superior Court since 2013; Washington State Supreme Court Justice Pro Tem; elected Superior Court Judges’ Association President by judges statewide; Chief of King County’s Family Law and Criminal Departments; Special Inquiry Judge; mental health court lead judge; prosecutor for 12 years, served on the Green River Task Force and tried Washington’s first human trafficking case; Special Assistant United States Attorney; statewide court security task force chair.

statement.label: Other professional experience
paragraphs: Adjunct Faculty, Seattle University School of Law

statement.label: Education
paragraphs: Seattle University School of Law, J.D. cum laude; Georgetown University, B.A.

statement.label: Community service
paragraphs: Rainier Scholars Resource Council; volunteer mediator; volunteer mock trial judge

statement.label: Statement
paragraphs: I have been in public service for 25 years as a trial judge, Supreme Court Justice Pro Tem, and prosecutor. I have protected individuals’ constitutional rights, upheld the rule of law, and centered crime victims' voices in our justice system.

I know the role the law plays to protect and serve us all. I began my legal career helping bring the Green River Killer to justice. As Chief Family Law Judge, I helped start a protection order court that resulted in hundreds of firearms being surrendered by people who committed acts of domestic violence. We live in unprecedented times for our democracy. As a Justice, I will defend our rights and the Constitution, maintain impartiality, and always remember that my rulings affect real people.

I am proud to be rated “Exceptionally Well Qualified” for the Supreme Court by multiple bar associations and named “Judge of the Year” by the Washington Chapter of the American Board of Trial Advocates.

Endorsements: Governor Christine Gregoire, Congressman Adam Smith, Congresswoman Marilyn Strickland, Lands Commissioner Dave Upthegrove, Seattle City Council President Joy Hollingsworth, 15 mayors, county executives, Washington Farm Bureau, Washington Council of Police and Sheriffs, and over 200 trial and appellate court judicial officers.

statement.label: Legal/judicial experience

statement.label: Other professional experience
paragraphs: Throughout career, led Appellate and Intellectual Property teams, and pro bono cases representing immigrant children, veterans, refugees, small businesses, and people experiencing homelessness.

statement.label: Education
paragraphs: BA, Claremont McKenna College; MA, Oxford University; MA, London School of Economics; JD, Yale University

statement.label: Community service
paragraphs: Trustee, King County Bar Association; President, Middle Eastern Legal Association of Washington; Member, Attorney General's Youth Internet Safety Task Force; Founders Award, Kids in Need of Defense; ACLU Humanitarian Award; Mentor of the Year, King County Bar Association

statement.label: Statement
paragraphs: As a Justice and throughout my legal career, I’ve fought for the rule of law, the rights of all individuals, and to ensure our courts remain fair, independent, and accessible. Before joining the Supreme Court, I frequently volunteered to help people who couldn’t afford lawyers. I sued the federal government when they forced children—as young as 4 years old—to appear without lawyers in immigration court. The federal government eventually agreed to pay for lawyers, and the ACLU gave me the Humanitarian Award.

I also represented an Army veteran, a naturalized U.S. citizen, after ICE wrongly detained him for seven months. The Northwest Immigrant Rights Project gave me the Amicus Award for my “groundbreaking work”.
I’ve worked to mentor attorneys to expand diversity in our profession, and with Turkish and Greek ancestry, I am proud to be the first Justice of Middle Eastern descent on our highest court.

I am endorsed by all of my colleagues on the Supreme Court; Governors Ferguson and Gregoire; former U.S. Attorneys Durkan, Gorman, and McKay; over 500 Judges and attorneys statewide; 52 State Legislators; Executive Zahilay; mayors statewide; WA State Labor Council; King County and numerous LD Democrats; and more!

statement.label: Legal/judicial experience
paragraphs: 41 years legal experience; trial judge (18 years, Ret.), trial lawyer (23 years). Rated AV Preeminent as a trial lawyer and Exceptionally Well Qualified (Judge and Supreme Court candidate).

statement.label: Other professional experience
paragraphs: Mediator and arbitrator (1990-2008); President, Federal Way School Board

statement.label: Education
paragraphs: JD, Seattle University School of Law; BA, University of Puget Sound.

statement.label: Community service
paragraphs: DMCJA President’s Award for Protecting Judicial Independence (2018); Judge William Nevins Award (2014) and Hero of Federal Way Schools (2018, 2022) for Commitment to Civics Education; Best City Leader (2022); Kiwanis (Everyday Hero Award and more); Founder, Aktion Club of Federal Way (service club for adults with developmental disabilities), and more.

statement.label: Statement
paragraphs: Judge Dave Larson's 41 years of distinguished experience, 18 years as a trial judge, 23 as a trial lawyer, form an unrivaled record making him the most qualified and best prepared candidate for our state’s highest court.

Dave will restore trust in our courts by rising above partisan interests, applying the law without fear or favor, and restoring judicial independence. A truly nonpartisan candidate, Dave reaches out to Democrats, Republicans, Labor, Business, and voters across Eastern and Western Washington, because justice that serves only some of us serves none of us. He will protect your individual rights and the judicial independence that is currently under threat.

Dave’s innovative criminal justice reforms have been recognized nationwide. He has collaborated with legislative Democrats and Republicans to help our trial courts address crime and addiction with compassion and accountability. However, our Supreme Court’s decisions have weakened that response. As a justice, he will help fix current problems and build towards lasting and effective solutions.

Our Supreme Court needs Dave’s unique perspective gained from his significant trial judge experience. That experience, integrity, and steady judgment are exactly what’s needed to restore trust in, and improve, our courts. Vote Judge Dave Larson for Supreme Court.

statement.label: Legal/judicial experience
paragraphs: Current Chief Justice and Justice since 2008. Court of Appeals Judge, Eastern Washington (2007). Appellate Attorney & adjunct professor, Gonzaga University (1993-2007).

statement.label: Other professional experience
paragraphs: Board for Judicial Administration Co-Chair, National Association of Women Judges, Judicial Independence Committee Co-Chair, Chief Justices Conference Executive Committee, National Courts & Sciences Institute Director, National Judicial College Instructor, WA Civic Learning Council, former Spokane Community College instructor.

statement.label: Education
paragraphs: Gonzaga University, J.D., B.A. West Valley High, Spokane.

statement.label: Community service

statement.label: Statement
paragraphs: As Washington’s Chief Justice, I am dedicated to upholding the rule of law and delivering fair and impartial justice. Courts are a critical branch of government, where every person must be treated fairly and with dignity, and decisions must be based on the law and the facts. In an era of growing attempts to politicize the judiciary, I work every day to maintain the integrity and independence of our courts and safeguard access to justice for every person.

As a former constitutional law professor, I respect legal traditions and constitutional principles. As a parent and former school board chair, I understand how court decisions impact the lives of Washington families. As the first woman from Eastern Washington on the Court, I know that lived experience and diverse perspectives matter in making sound decisions.

I have a proven record of expanding access to justice, improving efficiency and transparency, addressing the evolving challenges facing our legal system, and protecting individual rights. I have always enjoyed broad support and am endorsed by my current and former colleagues, judges statewide, WA State Labor Council, elected officials, and education and community leaders. I ask for your vote to continue serving you on our Supreme Court.

statement.label: Legal/judicial experience
paragraphs: Over two decades of providing legal and professional services to private and publicly-held companies, executives, business owners and Washington families; served as an Arbitrator for FINRA from 1999 to 2020.

statement.label: Other professional experience
paragraphs: Over a decade as tax attorney and senior manager in major accounting firms. Active-duty Navy officer from 2002 to 2013. Additional professional designations: CPA, CFA and CFP.

statement.label: Education
paragraphs: LL.M. - University of Washington; J.D., M.B.A. - Tulane University; M.A. - Naval War College; B.A. - Simpson College; College of Naval Command & Staff; Warfare Qualified.

statement.label: Community service
paragraphs: WSBA - Board of Governors; Nonprofit Finance Council; Adjunct faculty (UW, Tulane); Gallon+ Blood Donor

statement.label: Statement
paragraphs: Throughout my career, I've worked to solve complex problems thoughtfully, collaboratively, and fairly. And my background has given me a deep appreciation for hard work, sacrifice, and the experiences of everyday people. To pay for school, I worked farm, grocery and restaurant jobs and later earned my commission from the enlisted ranks.

Following 9/11, I was called from the Naval Reserve to active duty, where I served for more than a decade. I placed my civilian career on hold and left my wife and children to deploy to the Persian Gulf. That experience had a big impact on my understanding of duty, accountability, and leadership under pressure. Since returning to civilian life, I've continued my public service through the WSBA Board of Governors. It was there, I was encouraged to seek election to the Supreme Court.

This year's election is a choice--whether to retain the current justices or to give someone new your vote. I believe I represent meaningful new perspective, experience, and common sense which will bring balance to the court.
If elected, I promise to uphold and apply the law impartially and fairly. I respectfully ask for your vote for Supreme Court Justice, Position #7.

Successfully argued a landmark Freedom of Information Act case before the U.S. Supreme Court.

statement.label: Community service

statement.label: Statement
paragraphs: Judge David Mann was appointed by Governor Jay Inslee to the State Court of Appeals in 2016, elected to retain his position in 2017, and re-elected in 2020. He has served as the Chief Judge for Division I and is currently the most senior judge on the ten-member court. He is also a member of the State Board of Judicial Administration.

Following a career as a geophysicist, Judge Mann earned a law degree 35 years ago and began a successful practice as an environmental and land use lawyer. His skill, depth of knowledge, and commitment to our Northwest values, benefited citizens’ groups, tribes, and individual property owners across the state. He argued significant cases before state and Federal courts, including a successful Freedom of Information Action appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court.

Most cases appealed from Superior Courts go directly to the Court of Appeals, and the Court must accept all appeals filed. Judge Mann has proven himself to be a hard-working member of the judiciary, authoring more than 65 opinions each year dealing with every area of Washington law. He is endorsed by a majority of the current appellate judges and justices in the state.

Judge Bowman held several leadership roles on the King County Superior Court bench and worked collaboratively with his judicial colleagues and community groups to make important resources available to underserved parts of King County and safely reduce pretrial incarceration.

He is currently Acting Chief Judge for Division One and serves as Chair of the Court of Appeals Legislative Committee. At King County Superior Court, Judge Bowman served as Assistant Presiding Judge, Chief Judge of the Maleng Regional Justice Center, Chief Judge of the Civil Department and Assistant Chief Judge of the Criminal Department. He also chaired the Technology and Budget committees and served for several years on the Executive Committee.

Judge Bowman grew up in Laurel, Washington and graduated from Sehome High School. He currently lives on a small farm with his wife in south King County and enjoys running the trails of the Cascades and surfing the breaks in Westport.

statement.label: Statement
paragraphs: As King County’s first woman and first person of color to serve as Prosecutor, I have spent the past four years fulfilling my promise to keep our neighborhoods safe, reduce property crime, and protect survivors and the most vulnerable. Keeping that commitment requires proven vision, hands-on leadership and experience – qualities I possess and have strengthened since entering office.

Under my leadership, the Prosecutor’s Office prosecutes violent crimes, sexual assaults, and property crimes daily. Since my election, I have expanded support for survivors of domestic violence and sexual assault, invested in alternative sentencing for veterans, youth, and individuals facing behavioral health and addiction challenges, and prioritized juvenile justice reform.

My commitment to reducing gun violence shows in a nearly 50% reduction in gun homicides since 2023. I also worked to enact Washington’s strongest Extreme Risk Protection Order policies, a statewide ban on high-capacity magazines and ghost guns, and tools that help law enforcement track weapons used in crime.

I am proud of the work accomplished over the past four years: developing fair and effective criminal justice policies and reforms, leading a team of nearly 600 professionals, building trusted partnerships with law enforcement, public defenders, business and community leaders, and advocates for equity and justice. There is still important work to do, and I am ready to continue to ensure that our county is safe for everyone.

I am proudly endorsed by former Governors Gary Locke and Christine Gregoire; Executive Girmay Zahilay; former Seattle Mayor Bruce Harrell; the Alliance for Gun Responsibility; labor unions, King County Democrat organizations; dozens of county and city leaders; retired justices; and former U.S. Attorneys.

statement.label: Education
paragraphs: University of Washington, B.A.; Certified General Real Estate Appraiser; Seattle Public Schools graduate

statement.label: Occupation
paragraphs: Senior Appraiser, City of Seattle; Former King County Hearing Examiner

statement.label: Statement
paragraphs: The Assessor's office touches every person's ability to stay in their home. Rising property taxes are pushing homeowners, renters, and small businesses out of their communities, and too many people don't trust that the system is treating them fairly. King County needs an accurate, fair, and transparent Assessor's office that works for everyone.

I'm a fifth-generation Seattleite and the only candidate in this race who has actually done the valuation work this office depends on. As Senior Appraiser for the City of Seattle, I appraise public properties daily, ensuring real estate decisions serve the public interest. My career has included commercial valuation in the private sector. Serving as a Hearing Examiner on the King County Board of Appeals and Equalization, I've sat across the table from homeowners fighting to stay in their communities while corporate landowners brought teams of experts to secure tax reductions. I understand both sides of this system.
I've lived in income-restricted housing. I know what financial pressure looks like from the inside, and it's why I'm a proud PROTEC17 shop steward.

I'll bring real relief for homeowners and renters, and transparency and accountability to a system many people don't fully understand. In Olympia, I'll push to establish homestead protections for primary residences to help homeowners manage rising costs, and create a renter's tax credit to give tenants relief from rising housing costs as well.

I'm proud to be endorsed by the Seattle Times, the Stranger, King County Executive Girmay Zahilay, Chief Deputy Assessor Al Dams, King County Councilmembers Claudia Balducci, Sarah Perry, and Rhonda Lewis, King County Democrats, eleven legislative district Democratic organizations, Seattle Councilmembers Eddie Lin and Dionne Foster, multiple labor unions, and Danny Hagen, President of the Washington State Association of County Assessors, among others. They trust my professional expertise to lead this department.

statement.label: Education
paragraphs: B.A. Criminal Justice, Washington State University

statement.label: Occupation
paragraphs: Small Family Business Owner, CAPR King County Chapter President

statement.label: Statement
paragraphs: The King County Assessor is far more than an appraiser—it’s absolutely a leadership role, of one of the largest public offices affecting every property owner. While the office does employ appraisal staff, the Assessor's responsibility ensures the entire system operates transparently, consistently, fairly, and in accordance with the law.

I have studied our property tax system from the taxpayers perspective, analyzing assessment data, researching mass appraisal practices, public records requests, appealing assessments, reviewing BoE decisions, and developed comprehensive audit proposals identifying significant areas for reform. That experience gives me something many candidates cannot claim: a taxpayer's perspective on how the system actually functions in practice.

My campaign isn’t about making minor adjustments to the status quo. It’s about pursuing meaningful, system-wide reforms that protect taxpayers, strengthen property rights, ensures due process and helps ensure people aren’t taxed out of their homes.

Government should be judged by results—not intentions. Our current assessment system is required to produce fair and uniform assessments, but if that system does not produce the results required by law, we have a responsibility to examine it honestly, measure its performance, and improve it.

Property owners deserve information they can understand. They deserve parcel-specific breakdowns on their individual property valuations—not simply a final number. They deserve due process, timely appeals and logical evidentiary standards, and should never need to become valuation experts or pay for professional help, simply to challenge their assessment.

I’m a King County resident, small business owner, and President of the King County CAPR chapter. I’m not a politician. Government works best being fully transparent and accountable, and we demand fiscal responsibility. I will continue to work relentlessly to change the status quo, strengthen taxpayer protections, and advocate for significant reforms that restore fairness and accountability in one of King County’s most important public offices.

statement.label: Occupation

statement.label: Statement
paragraphs: Thank you for entrusting me to lead the Department of Elections for the past decade. In that time, we have added more than 80 secure ballot drop boxes, in-person voting centers, election materials in four new languages, ballot alerts, and new layers of physical and cybersecurity. We have also implemented national award-winning programs like the Voter Education Fund, our Civic Engagement Internship, and a robust Bipartisan Observer Program.

My parents instilled a sense of responsibility in my sister and me to contribute to our community and serve a greater purpose. In fact, it was when my father was running for Mayor of Enumclaw that I saw and applied for a job at the Department of Elections, twenty-six years ago. I fell in love with the work – ensuring every eligible voter could have their voice heard and working to protect one of our most critical institutions.

I remain just as passionate and committed today to improving our voting experience and maintaining a steadfast, transparent, and nonpartisan elections department. From Olympia to D.C., I will continue to advocate to ensure every person has meaningful access to their right to vote.
Thank you for voting!

statement.label: Occupation
paragraphs: B.A. Humanities and Theology, Seattle University

statement.label: Statement
paragraphs: I’m running for King County Council to build more housing that is affordable at any income, raise wages, improve transit, and make universal childcare a reality. Making King County a place every family can afford will require transformational change, and that’s exactly what I have been doing in the state senate for a decade.

Too many families are choosing between paying for rent or health insurance. As the daughter of a formerly undocumented Mexican farmworker, I will never stop fighting to protect our communities from masked ICE agents terrorizing our neighbors and corporations stealing our wages.

In the state senate, I championed and passed taxes on the ultra-wealthy, including the Capital Gains Tax and Millionaires Tax, to fund the essential services we need. As Labor Committee Chair, I passed the most progressive Paid Family and Medical Leave programs in the country and passed a Domestic Workers Bill of Rights to ensure fairness and dignity for care workers. I also delivered on landmark investments in affordable housing, transit, and community investments.

I’m proud to have earned the sole endorsement of the King County Democrats. I’ll bring new energy and proven leadership to the council to expand behavioral health and crisis response, improve transit access, and lower costs for working families. Addressing our toughest challenges will mean standing up to powerful special interests and never compromising on our values. That’s what I’ve spent my life doing.

Endorsements: King County Councilmembers Mosqueda, Perry, Balducci, and Gossett (fmr); Seattle City Councilmembers Foster, Hollingsworth, and Lin; progressive legislators Scott, Macri, Farivar, Street, and Javier Valdez; unions representing essential workers (SEIU 775, SEIU 925, and UFCW 3000); county employees (PROTEC17; Teamsters 28, 117, 174, and 763; and AFSCME Council 2); machinists (IAM 751); graduate students (UAW 6); more at rebeccasaldana.com!

statement.label: Education
paragraphs: Seattle University Masters, Criminal Justice; Bachelors, Criminal Justice; Bachelors, Spanish; Garfield High School; Kimball Elementary

statement.label: Occupation
paragraphs: Port of Seattle Commissioner; Small Business Owner, Agency Executive Director

statement.label: Statement
paragraphs: As a fourth generation Japanese American and mom of two, I’m proud to raise my family in the same Beacon Hill home my grandparents bought after being released from WWII concentration camps. But the fight to stay rooted here is harder than ever. Too many neighbors leave because politicians haven’t made affordability the priority. I believe everyone should be able to live in the place they love and call home. I’m ready to take this fight to the next level.

I served on transition teams for Governor Ferguson, Executive Zahilay and Mayor Wilson because they trust my expertise and ability to deliver. Now, King County must deliver the housing, childcare and transportation infrastructure people need.

As Port Commissioner, I championed childcare solutions, job opportunities, and delivered over $5,000,000,000 in capital projects on-time and on-budget. Before the Port Commission, I worked at King County where I served vulnerable communities by advancing equity and building accountability systems. I understand the county and where the opportunities are for improvement, I have delivered real reforms, and I am uniquely prepared to meet the needs of our communities.

As your next County Councilmember, I’ll champion anti-displacement protections for renters and home owners alike. I’ll fight for affordable, accessible childcare options for families and demand investments into transportation safety infrastructure to prevent deaths. I’ll prioritize upstream investments that get better outcomes for health and public safety. That means fully funding mental health and community-led gun violence prevention strategies, like after school and mentorship programs.

I’m endorsed by Executive Girmay Zahilay, City Attorney Erika Evans, County Councilmember Teresa Mosqueda, City Councilmembers Alexis Mercedes Rinck, Eddie Lin and Joy Hollingsworth, Governor Inslee, legislators, labor unions, Democratic organizations, and over 100 progressive District 2 community leaders. Let’s choose a better future.

statement.label: Occupation
